sentence meaning: We have a lot of things to do.

notes: Placed before a noun, usually with 的: 所有的人 (suǒyǒu de rén) “all the people.”
Object decides the sense: 开门 (kāi mén) “open [a door]”; 开车 (kāi chē) “drive”; 开灯 (kāi dēng) “turn on [a light].”
Placed after a verb to mark a brief/softened action: 看一下 (kàn yīxià) “take a quick look.”
Stronger than 很 (hěn); both go before adjectives or verbs like 喜欢 (xǐhuān).
到 after 看 marks successful perception. With 不/没: 看不到 (kàn bù dào) “can’t see”; 没看到 (méi kàndào) “didn’t see.”
Can be a verb or a noun: 有希望 (yǒu xīwàng) “there is hope.”
Casual “OK/works” for acceptability. Different from 可以 (kěyǐ, permission) and 能 (néng, ability).

sentence meaning: The day before, we saw him.
notes: Before a time word/measure, 前 means “previous, earlier” — e.g. 前一天 (qián yì tiān) “the day before.” As a location noun after 在, it means “in front” — e.g. 他在前 (tā zài qián) “he is in front.”

sentence meaning: I think this isn’t a big problem.
notes: More reasoned/formal than 觉得 (juéde) “to feel/think” in everyday talk.

Before a verb, 将 (jiāng) marks future or planned action. In formal style it can mean “to take” in a disposal pattern — e.g., 将它拿走 (jiāng tā ná zǒu) “take it away.” Also read jiàng, meaning “general (military rank)” — e.g., 上将 (shàngjiàng) “general.”
Colloquial for “here”; 这里 (zhèlǐ) is slightly more formal/neutral. Both mean the same.

sentence meaning: I’ve been waiting here for you the whole time.
notes: As a direction with a motion verb, 一直 means “straight (ahead)” — e.g., 一直走 (yìzhí zǒu) “go straight ahead.”

sentence meaning: Come take a look at this.
notes: Reduplicated verbs (V-V) mean “do briefly/try” and soften tone — 看看 (kànkan) “have a quick look.”

sentence meaning: When I get home, I’ll tell you.
notes: Placed after a clause, 时 (shí) means “when” in a somewhat formal style — e.g., 我到家时 (wǒ dào jiā shí) “when I get home.” 时候 (shíhòu) is the more common spoken form.
